1:3.t: "Tent of meeting": the KJV's "tabernacle of the congregation", the tent where God met with His people; see 1 Chronicles 6:32.

1:6.t: "Tent of meeting": the KJV's "tabernacle of the congregation", the tent where God met with His people; see 1 Chronicles 6:32.

1:13.t: "Tent of meeting": the KJV's "tabernacle of the congregation", the tent where God met with His people; see 1 Chronicles 6:32.

1:5.t: Bezalel: the KJV spells it Bezaleel. "Sought the LORD there": the KJV's "sought unto it"; the Hebrew can mean they sought the altar or sought the LORD. The verb darash means to seek, inquire of, or search out, and to seek the LORD is to turn to Him for guidance and worship (see 1 Chronicles 10:13-14).

1:8.t: "Great steadfast love": the KJV's "great mercy" (Hebrew hesed). hesed is loyal, committed love that keeps its promises, especially within a covenant; the KJV uses "mercy", "kindness" and "lovingkindness", and this translation uses "steadfast love" for God's hesed; see Genesis 24:27.

1:10.t: "Lead this people": the KJV's "go out and come in before this people", an idiom for leading them in daily life and in war. "Govern": the KJV's "judge", which in Hebrew covers ruling as well as deciding cases.

1:11.t: "Those who hate you": the KJV's "thine enemies".

1:14.t: Compare 1 Kings 10:26-29. 1 Kings 4:26 reads 40,000 stalls of horses, where 9:25 here reads 4,000; one figure probably comes from a copying error.

1:15.t: "Sycamore-fig trees of the western foothills": the KJV's "sycomore trees that are in the vale". The sycamore-fig is a kind of fig, not the American sycamore, and the western foothills are the Shephelah between the hill country and the coast; see 1 Chronicles 27:28.

1:16.t: "Linen yarn": as in the KJV. The Hebrew word is now generally read as Kue, the region of Cilicia in what is now southern Turkey, so many modern Bibles read "from Egypt and Kue".

1:17.t: KJV: "six hundred shekels of silver" and "an hundred and fifty". "Aram": the KJV's "Syria".

2:1.t: "A royal palace": the KJV's "an house for his kingdom".

2:2.t: "Assigned": the KJV's "told out", meaning counted off.

2:18.t: "Assigned": the KJV's "told out", meaning counted off.

2:3.t: Huram: the KJV's spelling here of Hiram (1 Kings 5).

2:4.t: "A lasting duty": the KJV's "an ordinance for ever".

2:6.t: "The highest heaven": the KJV's "heaven of heavens".

2:7.t: "Blue yarn": the KJV's "blue", a dye. "Skilled": the KJV's "cunning".

2:14.t: "Blue yarn": the KJV's "blue", a dye. "Skilled": the KJV's "cunning".
"From the tribe of Dan": 1 Kings 7:14 says his mother was a widow of the tribe of Naphtali. She may have been born in one tribe and lived in the other.

2:8.t: "Cypress": the KJV's "fir trees"; the Hebrew berosh is probably cypress or juniper. "Algum": a valuable wood, perhaps red sandalwood.

2:10.t: KJV: "twenty thousand measures" of wheat and of barley (the Hebrew cor) and "twenty thousand baths" of wine and of oil.

2:13.t: "Huram-abi": the KJV reads "of Huram my father's", taking abi, "my father", as a word rather than part of the name. 1 Kings 7:13 calls him Hiram.

2:17.t: "Foreigners": the KJV's "strangers", non-Israelites living in the land; see 1 Chronicles 22:2.

3:1.t: Mount Moriah: the same name as the place where Abraham was to offer Isaac (Genesis 22:2). "The LORD": the KJV prints "the Lord" here, but the Hebrew has no divine name in this clause, and many read "where He appeared". Ornan is called Araunah in 2 Samuel 24 (see 1 Chronicles 21:15).

3:3.t: KJV: "threescore cubits, and the breadth twenty cubits". "The old standard of measure": the KJV's "after the first measure"; the older cubit was a little longer than the one in use later.

3:4.t: KJV: "twenty cubits" and "an hundred and twenty". Some Greek and Syriac copies read twenty cubits for the height.

3:5.t: "Main hall": the KJV's "the greater house", the holy place in front of the inner room. "Paneled": the KJV's "cieled", lined with boards.

3:6.t: Parvaim: a gold-producing region whose location is unknown.

3:8.t: "Most Holy Place": the KJV's "the most holy house". KJV: "twenty cubits" and "six hundred talents".

3:10.t: "Sculptured": the KJV's "of image work"; the Hebrew word is uncertain.

3:13.t: "Their faces were turned inward": as in the KJV. The Hebrew says "toward the house", which many modern Bibles take as facing the main hall.

3:14.t: "Curtain": the KJV's "vail", the curtain before the Most Holy Place.

3:15.t: KJV: "thirty and five cubits high" and "five cubits". 1 Kings 7:15 gives eighteen cubits each; Chronicles may give the total length of both pillars. "Capital": the KJV's "chapiter".

3:16.t: "As in the inner sanctuary": the KJV's "as in the oracle". The KJV's "oracle" is the Most Holy Place, from the Hebrew debir. A slight change to the Hebrew gives "like a necklace", as some modern Bibles read.

3:17.t: Jachin probably means "He establishes", and Boaz "in Him is strength".

4:1.t: KJV: "twenty cubits the length thereof, and twenty cubits the breadth thereof, and ten cubits the height thereof". 1 Kings does not give the altar's size.

4:2.t: KJV: "ten cubits from brim to brim", "five cubits", "a line of thirty cubits".

4:3.t: "Figures of oxen": 1 Kings 7:24 has "knops", gourd-shaped ornaments; the two Hebrew words look alike. KJV: "ten in a cubit".

4:5.t: KJV: "an handbreadth" thick and "three thousand baths". 1 Kings 7:26 reads 2,000 baths.

4:16.t: "Polished bronze": the KJV's "bright brass". Huram-abi: the KJV's "Huram his father", taking abi, "my father" or "his father", as a word rather than part of the name; see 2:13.

4:17.t: "Clay molds": the KJV's "clay ground". Zeredah: the KJV's Zeredathah; 1 Kings 7:46 has Zarethan.

4:21.t: "Wick trimmers", "firepans": the KJV's "snuffers" and "censers". "Inner doors": the KJV's "the inner doors thereof for the most holy place".

5:3.t: "The feast in the seventh month": the Feast of Booths (Tabernacles), held in September and October. 1 Kings 8:2 names the month Ethanim.

5:9.t: "To this day": the writer copies these words from his source (1 Kings 8:8); the ark was lost when Jerusalem fell (36:18-19).

5:10.t: "Covenant": the KJV's "when the LORD made a covenant"; the Hebrew says only "when the LORD cut", the usual idiom for making a covenant.

5:11.t: "Without keeping to their divisions": the KJV's "did not then wait by course"; all the priests served at once instead of in their weekly turns (1 Chronicles 24).

5:13.t: "His steadfast love endures forever": the KJV's "his mercy endureth for ever". hesed is loyal, committed love that keeps its promises, especially within a covenant; the KJV uses "mercy", "kindness" and "lovingkindness", and this translation uses "steadfast love" for God's hesed. This refrain runs through Chronicles and every verse of Psalm 136; see 1 Chronicles 16:34.

6:1.t: Solomon's prayer follows 1 Kings 8:12-50 closely; 6:13, the platform, is added in Chronicles.

6:13.t: "Platform": the KJV's "scaffold". KJV: "five cubits long, and five cubits broad, and three cubits high".

6:14.t: "Steadfast love": the KJV's "mercy" (Hebrew hesed). hesed is loyal, committed love that keeps its promises, especially within a covenant; the KJV uses "mercy", "kindness" and "lovingkindness", and this translation uses "steadfast love" for God's hesed; see Genesis 24:27.

6:18.t: "The highest heaven": the KJV's "the heaven of heavens", meaning the very highest heaven; see 2:6.

6:22.t: "Required to take an oath": the KJV's "an oath be laid upon him to make him swear", an oath of innocence before God when there were no witnesses (Exodus 22:10-11).

6:28.t: "Blight": the KJV's "blasting", crops scorched by hot wind. "Grasshoppers": the KJV's "caterpillers"; the Hebrew word is another name for a kind of locust.

6:37.t: "Come to their senses": the KJV's "bethink themselves", literally "bring back to their heart".

6:41.t: "Faithful people": the KJV's "saints" (Hebrew hasidim, related to hesed), those who are loyal to God. 6:41-42 are close to Psalm 132:8-10 and do not appear in 1 Kings 8.

6:42.t: "Your steadfast love for David": the KJV's "the mercies of David". The Hebrew can mean God's steadfast love promised to David (as in Isaiah 55:3) or David's own loyal deeds; the first is followed here. "Do not turn away from Your anointed one": the KJV's "turn not away the face of thine anointed", meaning do not reject his request.

7:3.t: "His steadfast love endures forever": the KJV's "his mercy endureth for ever". hesed is loyal, committed love that keeps its promises, especially within a covenant; the KJV uses "mercy", "kindness" and "lovingkindness", and this translation uses "steadfast love" for God's hesed. See 1 Chronicles 16:34.

7:6.t: "His steadfast love endures forever": the KJV's "his mercy endureth for ever". hesed is loyal, committed love that keeps its promises, especially within a covenant; the KJV uses "mercy", "kindness" and "lovingkindness", and this translation uses "steadfast love" for God's hesed. See 1 Chronicles 16:34.

7:5.t: 22,000 oxen and 120,000 sheep: the same numbers as 1 Kings 8:63.

7:7.t: "Grain offerings": the KJV's "meat offerings", where "meat" means food; this offering was of grain and flour. See 1 Chronicles 21:23.

7:8.t: "Lebo-hamath": the KJV's "the entering in of Hamath", which may be a town name; it marks the northern border (see 1 Chronicles 13:5). "The Brook of Egypt": the KJV's "the river of Egypt", the Wadi el-Arish on Egypt's border, not the Nile.

7:9.t: Fourteen days in all: seven for the dedication of the altar and seven for the Feast of Booths, followed by a closing assembly. 1 Kings 8:65-66 says he sent them away on the eighth day, apparently counting from the feast.

7:20.t: "Uproot Israel": the KJV's "pluck them up"; "them" means the people of Israel. "Object of scorn": the KJV's "byword".

7:21.t: "Which is now so exalted": the KJV's "which is high". The Hebrew may also mean "this house, which was so exalted, will become a ruin", as some ancient translations read.

8:2.t: "The cities that Huram had given him": 1 Kings 9:11-13 says Solomon gave twenty cities to Hiram, who did not like them. Chronicles may mean that Hiram gave them back.

8:3.t: Hamath-zobah: this conquest is not mentioned in Kings.

8:4.t: Tadmor: an oasis city in the Syrian desert, later Palmyra. 1 Kings 9:18 reads Tamar in the Hebrew text.

8:5.t: "Upper", "Lower": the KJV's "the upper" and "the nether". "Fortified cities": the KJV's "fenced cities", here and throughout.

8:8.t: "Conscripted for forced labor": the KJV's "make to pay tribute"; the Hebrew mas means forced labor.

8:10.t: 250 officials: 1 Kings 9:23 reads 550. The two books may count different ranks of supervisors.

8:13.t: "As the duty of each day required": the KJV's "after a certain rate every day". "Feast of Booths": the KJV's "feast of tabernacles", when Israel lived in shelters for a week (Leviticus 23:42).

8:14.t: "Gatekeepers": the KJV's "porters", meaning those who kept the doors and gates; see 1 Chronicles 9:17.

8:17.t: Eloth: Elath, on the Gulf of Aqaba.

8:18.t: KJV: "four hundred and fifty talents of gold". 1 Kings 9:28 reads 420 talents.

9:1.t: "Test": the KJV's "prove". "Talked with him about everything that was on her mind": the KJV's "communed with him of all that was in her heart".

9:4.t: "Stairway": the KJV's "ascent". 1 Kings 10:5 can be read "the burnt offerings he offered". "She was left breathless": the KJV's "there was no more spirit in her".

9:9.t: KJV: "an hundred and twenty talents of gold".

9:11.t: "Steps": the KJV's "terraces"; 1 Kings 10:12 has "pillars" or "supports". The Hebrew word is uncertain.

9:13.t: KJV: "six hundred and threescore and six talents of gold".

9:15.t: KJV: "six hundred shekels" and "three hundred shekels". 1 Kings 10:17 reads "three pounds" (manehs, about 1.7 kilograms) for the small shields. "Large shields": the KJV's "targets".

9:21.t: "Went to Tarshish": as in the KJV. 1 Kings 10:22 speaks of a "navy of Tarshish", a kind of large trading ship. "Peacocks": the Hebrew word is uncertain and may mean baboons or another animal.

9:25.t: 4,000 stalls: 1 Kings 4:26 reads 40,000 stalls; one figure probably comes from a copying error. See 1:14.

9:29.t: "Records": the KJV's "book"; the Hebrew dibre means words, acts or records (see 1 Chronicles 29:29). "Of Shiloh": the KJV's "the Shilonite".

9:31.t: "Rested with his fathers": the KJV's "slept with his fathers", a way of saying that he died, here and throughout.

10:7.t: "Kind": the Hebrew is tov, "good", not hesed. 1 Kings 12:7 reads "be a servant to this people".

10:11.t: "Scorpions": probably whips with metal points or barbs.

10:15.t: "This turn of events came from God": the KJV's "the cause was of God".

10:16.t: "Every man to your tents": an old battle cry meaning "Let us go home".

10:18.t: Hadoram: called Adoram in 1 Kings 12:18 and Adoniram in 1 Kings 4:6. "Forced labor": the KJV's "tribute"; the Hebrew mas means forced labor (see 8:8).

11:5.t: Of these fifteen fortified cities, most guard the roads into Judah from the south and west.

11:11.t: "Supplies of food": the KJV's "store of victual".

11:14.t: "Pasturelands": the KJV's "suburbs", meaning the open land around a town used for grazing; see 1 Chronicles 5:16.

11:15.t: "Goat idols": the KJV's "devils". The Hebrew seirim means "goats" or "hairy ones", goat-shaped idols or demons (Leviticus 17:7).

11:18.t: "And Abihail": the KJV's reading, which could mean a second wife. Many modern Bibles read "and of Abihail", naming Mahalath's mother, since the next verse speaks of only one wife ("she").

11:20.t: Maacah: the KJV's Maachah. "Daughter of Absalom": 13:2 names Abijah's mother Micaiah the daughter of Uriel. "Daughter" can mean granddaughter.

11:23.t: "Sought many wives for them": the KJV's "he desired many wives", which can be read of Rehoboam himself; the Hebrew says "he asked for a multitude of wives", most likely for his sons.

12:2.t: Shishak: Pharaoh Shoshenq I, whose own inscription lists towns he took in Judah and Israel, about 925 B.C.

12:3.t: Sukkites: the KJV's "Sukkiims", a people perhaps from the Libyan desert. "Libyans": the KJV's "Lubims". "Cushites": the KJV's "Ethiopians", people of the upper Nile, in what is now Sudan.

12:7.t: "Some deliverance": the Hebrew kimat can mean "a little" or "soon".

12:8.t: "Learn the difference between serving Me and serving the kingdoms": the KJV's "know my service, and the service of the kingdoms of the countries".

12:10.t: "Commanders of the guard": the KJV's "chief of the guard"; the Hebrew says "runners", royal escorts.

12:12.t: "There was still some good in Judah": the KJV's "in Judah things went well". The Hebrew can mean either.

"Humbled themselves" (Hebrew kana): kana means to bend low, to admit one's need before God; in Chronicles it marks the kings God spares (see 7:14). This is the first test of that promise: even a king who had abandoned the LORD is spared, in part, when he bows low.

12:15.t: "In the genealogies": the KJV's "concerning genealogies"; the Hebrew phrase is unclear.

13:1.t: Abijah: called Abijam in 1 Kings 15:1. Micaiah: the KJV's Michaiah; 1 Kings 15:2 has Maacah the daughter of Abishalom. "Daughter" can mean granddaughter, and Micaiah may be another form of Maacah's name; see 11:20.

13:3.t: 400,000 and 800,000: large, perhaps symbolic numbers, as are the 500,000 dead in 13:17. The Hebrew word for "thousand" may also mean a military unit.

13:5.t: "A covenant of salt": a lasting covenant. Salt preserves and was used in sacrifices and in sealing agreements (Numbers 18:19).

13:7.t: "Worthless men, scoundrels": the KJV's "vain men, the children of Belial". The Hebrew beliya'al probably means "without worth" or "good for nothing"; the KJV keeps it as if it were a name (see 1 Kings 21:10). "Timid": the KJV's "tenderhearted", meaning inexperienced and weak, not compassionate.

13:9.t: "Consecrate himself": literally "fill his hand", an idiom for ordaining a priest; see 1 Chronicles 29:5.

13:11.t: "Table of pure gold": the KJV's "pure table". "Charge": duties, the things the LORD gave them to keep.

13:12.t: "At our head": the KJV's "for our captain".

13:19.t: Ephrain: the KJV's spelling, following the Hebrew margin; the written Hebrew text reads Ephron. It is probably Ophrah.

13:20.t: Jeroboam outlived Abijah (1 Kings 15:9, 15:25); "he died" may refer to Jeroboam's later death, or the Hebrew "struck him" may refer to Abijah.

13:22.t: "Commentary": the KJV's "story"; the Hebrew midrash means a study or account.

14:3.t: "Foreign altars": the KJV's "the altars of the strange gods". "Sacred pillars": the KJV's "images", standing stones used in Canaanite worship. "Asherah poles": the KJV's "groves". Asherah was a Canaanite mother goddess, and her symbol was a wooden pole or carved tree set up beside an altar; see 1 Kings 14:15.

"Removed the high places": 15:17 and 20:33 say the high places were not removed. Chronicles may mean the shrines to other gods were removed while hilltop altars to the LORD stayed, or that the work was begun and not finished.

14:5.t: "Removed the high places": 15:17 and 20:33 say the high places were not removed. Chronicles may mean the shrines to other gods were removed while hilltop altars to the LORD stayed, or that the work was begun and not finished.
"Incense altars": the KJV's "images"; the Hebrew chammanim are probably incense stands.

17:6.t: "Removed the high places": 15:17 and 20:33 say the high places were not removed. Chronicles may mean the shrines to other gods were removed while hilltop altars to the LORD stayed, or that the work was begun and not finished.

"His heart was bold": the KJV's "his heart was lifted up", here in a good sense, meaning encouraged. On the high places: 20:33 says they were not removed. Chronicles may mean the shrines to other gods were removed while hilltop altars to the LORD stayed, or that the work was begun and not finished (see 14:3).

14:7.t: "The land is still ours": the KJV's "while the land is yet before us", meaning open to them, free of enemies.

"Seek" (Hebrew darash, also biqqesh in 15:4 and 15:15): darash means to seek, inquire of, or search out, and it is a key word in Chronicles: to seek the LORD is to turn to Him for guidance and to give Him one's worship and loyalty; to fail to seek Him is the heart of unfaithfulness (see 1 Chronicles 10:13-14). In Asa's story "seek" sounds again and again: the king calls Judah to seek the LORD, and the prophet promises that those who seek Him will find Him. When Asa later relies on Aram and seeks only physicians (16:7, 16:12), the same word marks his decline.

14:8.t: KJV: "three hundred thousand" and "two hundred and fourscore thousand". "Large shields", "small shields": the KJV's "targets" and "shields".

14:9.t: "Cushite": the KJV's "Ethiopian", from Cush, south of Egypt; Zerah may have led troops for Egypt. "A million": the KJV's "a thousand thousand", perhaps a way of saying a countless army.

14:11.t: "There is no one but You who can help, whether the powerful or the weak": the KJV's "it is nothing with thee to help, whether with many, or with them that have no power". The Hebrew can mean that only God can help the weak against the strong.

14:13.t: "So many Cushites fell that none of them were left alive": the KJV's "they could not recover themselves". "His army": the KJV's "his host", perhaps Judah's army or the armies of heaven.

14:14.t: "The terror of the LORD": the KJV's "the fear of the LORD", here meaning a dread sent by God on the enemy.

15:2.t: "He will let you find Him": the KJV's "he will be found of you", meaning God will let Himself be found by those who seek Him; see 1 Chronicles 28:9.

"Seek" (Hebrew darash, also biqqesh in 15:4 and 15:15): darash means to seek, inquire of, or search out, and it is a key word in Chronicles: to seek the LORD is to turn to Him for guidance and to give Him one's worship and loyalty; to fail to seek Him is the heart of unfaithfulness (see 1 Chronicles 10:13-14). In Asa's story "seek" sounds again and again: the king calls Judah to seek the LORD, and the prophet promises that those who seek Him will find Him. When Asa later relies on Aram and seeks only physicians (16:7, 16:12), the same word marks his decline.

15:4.t: "He will let you find Him": the KJV's "he will be found of you", meaning God will let Himself be found by those who seek Him; see 1 Chronicles 28:9.

15:15.t: "He will let you find Him": the KJV's "he will be found of you", meaning God will let Himself be found by those who seek Him; see 1 Chronicles 28:9.

15:3.t: This may describe the time of the judges, or speak in general of a people without God.

15:8.t: "The prophecy of Oded the prophet": as in the KJV; the Hebrew lacks "Azariah the son of", and some ancient translations supply it.

15:9.t: "Living among them": the KJV's "the strangers with them", resident foreigners from the northern tribes.

15:10.t: "The third month": Sivan, in May and June, the month of the Feast of Weeks.

15:13.t: This applied the law of Deuteronomy 13:6-10 and 17:2-5 to those who turned to other gods.

15:16.t: "His grandmother": the KJV's "the mother of Asa"; Maacah was Abijah's mother (11:20), and the Hebrew "mother" can mean grandmother. "Disgusting image": the KJV's "idol in a grove"; the Hebrew means a horrid thing made for Asherah. "Kidron Valley": the KJV's "the brook Kidron".

15:19.t: "The thirty-fifth year": 1 Kings 15:33 says Baasha reigned only twenty-four years, beginning in Asa's third year, so he died in Asa's twenty-sixth year. Some take this date, and the thirty-sixth year in 16:1, to count from the division of the kingdom; others think a copying error has crept in.

16:9.t: "Wholly devoted" (Hebrew shalem, the KJV's "perfect"): from the same root as shalom, which means wholeness and well-being (see 1 Chronicles 22:9). It means whole, complete, undivided, not sinless.

16:12.t: "He did not seek the LORD": the KJV's "he sought not to the LORD". The Hebrew darash means to seek, inquire of, or search out, and it is a key word in Chronicles: to seek the LORD is to turn to Him for guidance and to give Him one's worship and loyalty; to fail to seek Him is the heart of unfaithfulness (see 1 Chronicles 10:13-14). The writer does not fault him for using physicians, but for turning only to them.

16:14.t: "Tomb he had cut out": the KJV's "sepulchres, which he had made", tombs cut in rock. "Bier": the KJV's "bed". "A very great fire": a fire of spices burned in his honor, not a cremation (compare 21:19, Jeremiah 34:5).

17:3.t: "The earlier ways of his father David": the KJV's "the first ways of his father David". Some Hebrew copies lack "David", making it Asa's earlier ways. "The Baals": the KJV's "Baalim", the Hebrew plural, meaning local forms of Baal, the Canaanite storm and fertility god (baal means "lord" or "master"); see 1 Kings 16:31-32.

17:4.t: "Sought": the KJV's "sought to". The Hebrew darash means to seek, inquire of, or search out, and it is a key word in Chronicles: to seek the LORD is to turn to Him for guidance and to give Him one's worship and loyalty; to fail to seek Him is the heart of unfaithfulness (see 1 Chronicles 10:13-14).

17:7.t: Nethanel, Micaiah: the KJV spells them Nethaneel and Michaiah.

17:14.t: These numbers total 1,160,000, a very large army. They may be large or symbolic numbers, and the Hebrew word for "thousand" may also mean a military unit; see 13:3.

17:16.t: "Volunteered for the service of the LORD": the KJV's "willingly offered himself unto the LORD".

18:1.t: "Made an alliance by marriage": the KJV's "joined affinity". His son Jehoram married Ahab's daughter Athaliah (21:6).

18:9.t: "At the threshing floor": the KJV's "in a void place", an open space; the Hebrew goren means a threshing floor.

18:10.t: "Gore": the KJV's "push". Horns are a picture of strength.

18:16.t: "Go home in peace": the sheep without a shepherd point to the king's death in battle.

18:22.t: "Disaster": the KJV's "evil", meaning harm, not moral evil.

18:26.t: "Nothing but bread and water": the KJV's "bread of affliction and ... water of affliction", meaning short rations.

18:31.t: "God drew them away": Chronicles adds this to 1 Kings 22:32.

18:33.t: "At random": the KJV's "at a venture". "Armor": the KJV's "harness". "Chariot driver": the KJV's "chariot man".

19:2.t: "Wicked": the KJV's "ungodly". Jehoshaphat's alliance with Ahab (chapter 18) is meant.

19:7.t: "Favoritism": the KJV's "respect of persons". "Bribes": the KJV's "gifts".

19:8.t: "They lived in Jerusalem": the KJV's "when they returned to Jerusalem". The Hebrew is unclear; with a small change of vowels it reads "and they lived in Jerusalem", which is followed here.

19:10.t: "Bloodshed": the KJV's "between blood and blood", cases of killing, whether murder or accident. "Rules": the KJV's "judgments".

20:1.t: "Meunites": the KJV's "other beside the Ammonites". The Hebrew repeats "Ammonites", which does not make sense; the Greek Old Testament reads Meunites, a people from near Edom (26:7).

20:2.t: "The Dead Sea": the KJV's "the sea". "From Aram": as in the KJV's "on this side Syria". One Hebrew copy reads Edom, which differs from Aram by one letter and fits the setting better.

20:9.t: "The sword of judgment": the KJV's "the sword, judgment", which may be two things or one.

20:10.t: Israel was forbidden to attack these peoples on the way from Egypt (Deuteronomy 2:4-19).

20:16.t: "The Ascent of Ziz": the KJV's "the cliff of Ziz", a pass up from the Dead Sea near En-gedi. "Valley": the KJV's "brook".

20:17.t: "Stand firm, and see the salvation": compare Moses at the Red Sea (Exodus 14:13).

20:21.t: "In the beauty of holiness": kept from the KJV; it may also mean "in holy clothing", the festive dress of worship (see 1 Chronicles 16:29). "Give thanks": the KJV's "Praise"; the Hebrew hodu is the same word as in 1 Chronicles 16:34. "His steadfast love endures forever": the KJV's "his mercy endureth for ever"; hesed is loyal, committed love that keeps its promises, especially within a covenant; the KJV uses "mercy", "kindness" and "lovingkindness", and this translation uses "steadfast love" for God's hesed (see 1 Chronicles 16:34).

20:23.t: "Destroy them completely": the Hebrew verb is haram, "devote to destruction", to hand something over entirely to God so that nothing is kept for personal use; see 1 Chronicles 2:7.

20:25.t: "Among the dead bodies": the KJV's reading (Hebrew pegarim). Several Hebrew copies and the Latin read "clothing" (begadim), a one-letter difference. "Valuable things": the KJV's "precious jewels".

20:26.t: Beracah: the KJV's Berachah; the name means "blessing".

20:28.t: "Harps, lyres": the KJV's "psalteries and harps". Throughout Chronicles "lyres" stands for the KJV's "harps" (Hebrew kinnor) and "harps" for the KJV's "psalteries" (nebel); see 1 Chronicles 13:8.

20:31.t: Thirty-five and twenty-five years: the same as 1 Kings 22:42.

20:33.t: "The high places were not removed": compare 17:6 and the note at 14:3, which say Asa and Jehoshaphat removed them. Chronicles may mean the shrines to other gods were removed while hilltop altars to the LORD stayed, or that the work was begun and not finished.

20:34.t: "Records": the KJV's "book". "Which are recorded in": the KJV's "who is mentioned in"; the Hebrew says the record was taken up into the book of the kings.

20:35.t: 1 Kings 22:48-49 says that after the ships were wrecked, Jehoshaphat refused Ahaziah's offer to join him. "Ships to go to Tarshish": the KJV's phrase; 1 Kings 22:48 speaks of "ships of Tarshish", a kind of large trading ship, going to Ophir; see 9:21.

20:37.t: Dodavahu: the KJV's Dodavah. "Will destroy": the KJV's "hath broken", a prophetic past, as good as done.

21:2.t: "King of Israel": as in the Hebrew; Chronicles sometimes calls Judah "Israel", as the true people of God.

21:4.t: "Officials of Israel": the KJV's "princes of Israel", probably leaders in Judah.

21:7.t: "A lamp": the KJV's "a light", the promise that David's line would continue (1 Kings 11:36).

21:9.t: "Who had surrounded him": the KJV's reading. 2 Kings 8:21 suggests he broke out of an Edomite encirclement.

21:11.t: "Led ... to be unfaithful to God": the KJV's "to commit fornication", the Bible's common picture of idolatry as unfaithfulness in marriage; see 1 Chronicles 5:25.

21:12.t: A letter from Elijah: Elijah was taken up during the reign of Jehoshaphat (2 Kings 3:11 shows Elisha active then), so the letter may have been written before he was taken up, or the timing of 2 Kings 2 is not strictly in order.

21:16.t: "Anger": the KJV's "spirit". "Arabs": the KJV's "Arabians". "Cushites": the KJV's "Ethiopians", people of Cush, south of Egypt; see 14:9.

21:17.t: Jehoahaz: called Ahaziah in 22:1; the two names have the same parts in reverse order.

21:19.t: "Made no fire in his honor": a fire of spices was burned at a king's burial to honor him, not a cremation; Jehoram was denied it. See 16:14.

21:20.t: "With no one's regret": the KJV's "without being desired".

22:2.t: "Forty-two years old": as in the Hebrew. 2 Kings 8:26 reads twenty-two, and since his father died at forty (21:20), the Chronicles number is probably a copying error; some Greek copies read twenty, the Syriac twenty-two. "Granddaughter of Omri": the KJV's "daughter of Omri"; she was Ahab's daughter (21:6).

22:5.t: Joram and Jehoram: two spellings of the same name, used for the king of Israel.

22:6.t: Azariah: as in most Hebrew copies; the same person is Ahaziah (22:1-2), as some Hebrew copies read. "Ramah": short for Ramoth-gilead.

22:9.t: Compare 2 Kings 9:27-28, which says Ahaziah fled to Megiddo and died there and was buried in Jerusalem. "Grandson": the KJV's "son".

23:1.t: Compare 2 Kings 11:4-20, where the guards are the Carites and royal runners. Chronicles gives the roles to the priests and Levites, so that no one but the holy enter the temple.

23:5.t: "The Foundation Gate": the KJV's "the gate of the foundation"; 2 Kings 11:6 reads "the gate of Sur".

23:6.t: "Keep the LORD's command": the KJV's "keep the watch of the LORD", meaning stay where the Law placed them.

23:9.t: "Large and small shields": the KJV's "bucklers, and shields".

23:10.t: "South side ... north side": the KJV's "right side ... left side", facing east.

23:11.t: "The testimony": a copy of the covenant law, or a royal document; compare Deuteronomy 17:18. "Long live the king!": the KJV's "God save the king".

23:14.t: "Between the ranks": the KJV's "forth of the ranges".

23:20.t: "The Upper Gate": the KJV's "the high gate".

24:6.t: "Tax": the KJV's "collection", the half-shekel tax of Exodus 30:12-16. "Tent of the testimony": the KJV's "tabernacle of witness", the tent that held the tablets of the covenant.

24:7.t: "The Baals": the KJV's "Baalim", the Hebrew plural, meaning local forms of Baal, the Canaanite storm and fertility god (baal means "lord" or "master"); see 17:3.

24:10.t: "Until it was full": the KJV's "until they had made an end".

24:11.t: "Secretary": the KJV's "scribe", a royal official; see 1 Chronicles 18:16.

24:13.t: "The repairs went forward": the Hebrew says "healing went up on the work", meaning the damage was mended.

24:15.t: KJV: "an hundred and thirty years old".

24:18.t: "Asherah poles": the KJV's "groves". Asherah was a Canaanite mother goddess, and her symbol was a wooden pole or carved tree set up beside an altar; see 14:3. "Guilt": the KJV's "trespass".

24:20.t: "The Spirit of God came upon": the Hebrew says the Spirit "clothed" him, as with Gideon (Judges 6:34) and Amasai (1 Chronicles 12:18). Jesus may refer to this Zechariah in Matthew 23:35 and Luke 11:51, Chronicles being the last book of the Hebrew Bible. Matthew calls him "son of Barachiah", perhaps confusing or combining him with the prophet Zechariah (Zechariah 1:1).

24:22.t: "Kindness" (Hebrew hesed): loyal, committed love that keeps its promises; a person's hesed is rendered "kindness" (see Genesis 24:27). "Call you to account": the KJV's "require it".

24:24.t: "With only a few men": the reverse of 14:9-12 and 20:1-29, where a small Judah beat a vast army.

24:25.t: "Badly wounded": the KJV's "in great diseases". "Sons": the Hebrew and the KJV; the Greek and Latin read "son", meaning Zechariah.

24:26.t: Zabad and Shimrith: 2 Kings 12:21 has Jozachar and Shomer. Chronicles notes the mothers were Ammonite and Moabite.

24:27.t: "The many prophecies against him": the KJV's "the greatness of the burdens laid upon him"; the Hebrew massa can mean a burden or a prophetic oracle. "Commentary": the KJV's "story"; the Hebrew midrash means a study or account (see 13:22).

25:6.t: KJV: "an hundred thousand mighty men of valour" and "an hundred talents of silver".

25:7.t: "Not with any of the people of Ephraim": the KJV's "to wit, with all the children of Ephraim", the northern kingdom.

25:8.t: "Even if you go and fight bravely": the KJV's "But if thou wilt go, do it, be strong for the battle". The Hebrew is difficult; it may be ironic, "go, fight bravely; God will still make you fall".

25:11.t: "The Valley of Salt": the KJV's "the valley of salt", south of the Dead Sea. 2 Kings 14:7 gives the same 10,000.

25:12.t: "Cliff": the KJV's "rock"; the Hebrew sela may also be the Edomite city Sela (2 Kings 14:7).

25:16.t: "Royal adviser": the KJV's "of the king's counsel". The prophet's word "decided" plays on "counsel" and "advice": the king rejected the prophet's counsel, so God "counseled" to destroy him.

25:17.t: "Face each other in battle": the KJV's "see one another in the face", a challenge to fight.

25:23.t: "Ephraim Gate", "Corner Gate": gates on the north side of Jerusalem. KJV: "four hundred cubits".

25:24.t: "In the care of Obed-edom": a descendant of the gatekeeper Obed-edom (1 Chronicles 26:15), in charge of the storehouse.

25:28.t: "The city of Judah": the City of David, as 2 Kings 14:20 reads.

26:1.t: Uzziah: called Azariah in 2 Kings 14:21 and 15:1-7; see 1 Chronicles 3:12.

26:2.t: Eloth: Elath, on the Gulf of Aqaba (see 8:17).

26:5.t: "Who instructed him in the fear of God": as in many Hebrew copies and the Greek; the KJV's "who had understanding in the visions of God" follows the printed Hebrew, which differs by one letter.

26:7.t: "Arabs": the KJV's "Arabians". "Meunites": the KJV's "Mehunims", a people from near Edom; see 20:1.

26:8.t: "The border of Egypt": the KJV's "the entering in of Egypt".

26:10.t: "Cisterns": the KJV's "wells", tanks cut in rock to hold rainwater. "Western foothills ... plain": the KJV's "low country, and ... plains". "Fertile lands": the KJV's "Carmel", which may be the name of the mountain or the Hebrew word for a fruitful field. "He loved the soil": the KJV's "he loved husbandry".

26:13.t: KJV: "three hundred thousand and seven thousand and five hundred".

26:14.t: "Coats of armor": the KJV's "habergeons", coats of mail.

26:15.t: "Machines": the KJV's "engines", devices on the walls for shooting arrows and stones, or perhaps protective frames from which soldiers could shoot. "Skilled": the KJV's "cunning".

26:16.t: "His heart grew proud": the KJV's "his heart was lifted up"; compare 17:6, where the same phrase is used in a good sense, meaning encouraged. Only priests could burn incense (Exodus 30:7-8, Numbers 16:40).

26:19.t: "Leprosy": the KJV's word. The Hebrew tsaraat covers several skin diseases, not only what is now called leprosy (Leviticus 13).

26:21.t: "A separate house": the KJV's "a several house". The Hebrew may mean "a house of freedom", that is, released from duties. "Governing": the KJV's "judging". 2 Kings 15:5 tells the same.

26:23.t: "A burial field that belonged to the kings": he was buried near, not in, the royal tombs, because of his disease.

27:2.t: "He did not enter the temple": he did not repeat his father's sin (26:16).

27:3.t: Ophel: the hill on the southeast side of Jerusalem, between the City of David and the temple.

27:5.t: KJV: "an hundred talents of silver, and ten thousand measures of wheat, and ten thousand of barley"; the measure is the cor.

27:6.t: "Ordered his ways": the KJV's "prepared his ways".

28:2.t: "Cast metal images": the KJV's "molten images". "The Baals": the KJV's "Baalim", the Hebrew plural, meaning local forms of Baal, the Canaanite storm and fertility god (baal means "lord" or "master"); see 17:3.

28:3.t: "The Valley of the Son of Hinnom": a valley south of Jerusalem, later a place of child sacrifice; its Hebrew name Ge-hinnom gave rise to Gehenna. "Burned his sons in the fire": the KJV's "burnt his children in the fire"; 2 Kings 16:3 reads "made his son to pass through the fire".

28:5.t: Chronicles reports separate defeats by Aram and Israel; 2 Kings 16:5 and Isaiah 7:1 describe the two kings joining against Jerusalem.

28:7.t: "Officer in charge of the palace": the KJV's "governor of the house". "Second to the king": the KJV's "next to the king".

28:8.t: KJV: "two hundred thousand". "Relatives": the KJV's "brethren"; the people of Judah were their kin.

28:10.t: "Male and female slaves": the KJV's "bondmen and bondwomen". The Law forbade making fellow Israelites slaves (Leviticus 25:39-46).

28:15.t: "Named for the task": the KJV's "expressed by name". Jesus' parable of the good Samaritan echoes this scene (Luke 10:30-37).

28:16.t: "Kings of Assyria": as in the Hebrew; the Greek and 2 Kings 16:7 read "king".

28:18.t: "Negev": the KJV's "south", the dry land south of Judah. Aijalon, Soco: the KJV's Ajalon and Shocho.

28:19.t: "King of Israel": as in the Hebrew; Chronicles sometimes calls Judah "Israel", as the true people of God (see 21:2). "Let Judah run wild": the KJV's "made Judah naked"; the Hebrew may mean he threw off restraint.

28:20.t: Tiglath-pileser: the KJV's Tilgath-pilneser; see 1 Chronicles 5:6. 2 Kings 16:9 says he took Damascus, which helped Ahaz for a time, but Chronicles stresses the heavy cost.

28:23.t: "Who had defeated him": the KJV's "which smote him"; Ahaz thought the gods of Aram had given Aram the victory.

28:24.t: "Street corner": the KJV's "every corner of Jerusalem".

29:1.t: Abijah: the KJV's spelling; 2 Kings 18:2 has Abi.

29:3.t: "The first month": Nisan, in March and April. Hezekiah began to reform at once.

29:4.t: "The square on the east": the KJV's "the east street", an open space east of the temple.

29:8.t: "An object of terror, horror, and scorn": the KJV's "trouble, astonishment, and hissing", the last being the sound people made at a ruin.

29:17.t: "In eight more days": the KJV's "in eight days"; the work took sixteen days in all.

29:21.t: "Bulls": the KJV's "bullocks". "Male goats": the KJV's "he goats".

29:24.t: "Made a sin offering": the KJV's "made reconciliation"; the Hebrew verb is from chatta't, which means both "sin" and the offering that deals with sin, purifying the sanctuary and the worshiper (see Exodus 29:14). To make atonement means to remove guilt and defilement so that the relationship with God is restored (see Exodus 29:33).

29:25.t: "Harps, and lyres": the KJV's "psalteries, and ... harps". Throughout Chronicles "lyres" stands for the KJV's "harps" (Hebrew kinnor) and "harps" for the KJV's "psalteries" (nebel); see 1 Chronicles 13:8. The KJV's printed text here includes a stray margin note, "Heb. commandment by the hand of the LORD"; it is not part of the verse.

29:31.t: "Dedicated yourselves": the KJV's "consecrated yourselves", literally "filled your hand", an idiom for ordaining a priest, here used of giving; see 1 Chronicles 29:5. "Willing": the KJV's "of a free heart".

29:32.t: KJV: "threescore and ten bullocks, an hundred rams, and two hundred lambs"; "six hundred oxen and three thousand sheep".

29:34.t: "Skin": the KJV's "flay". "More conscientious": the KJV's "more upright in heart".

30:1.t: This Passover is not mentioned in Kings, though 2 Kings 23:22 notes that no Passover like Josiah's had been kept since the judges.

30:2.t: "The second month": the Law allowed those who were unclean or away at Passover time to keep it a month later (Numbers 9:10-11).

30:5.t: "In great numbers": the KJV's "of a long time"; the Hebrew lerov can mean "in large numbers" or "for a long time".

30:6.t: "Couriers": the KJV's "posts", runners carrying the king's letters. "Kings of Assyria": the northern kingdom had fallen to Assyria (2 Kings 17).

"Return" (Hebrew shuv): the basic meaning is to turn around or come back; the same verb describes turning back to God in repentance and returning home from exile (see 1 Kings 8:47-48 and 7:14). The letter plays on the word: if the people return to the LORD, He will return to them, and their captive relatives will return to the land.

30:8.t: "Do not be stubborn": the KJV's "be ye not stiffnecked". "Submit to": the KJV's "yield yourselves unto", literally "give the hand to".

30:9.t: "Gracious and merciful": these words quote God's description of Himself in Exodus 34:6. Gracious (hannun) means showing undeserved favor; merciful (rahum) is related to the word for womb, a tender compassion. See Nehemiah 9:17.

30:14.t: "Incense altars": the KJV's "altars for incense"; see 28:24-25.

30:17.t: "Ceremonially clean": clean by the rules of worship, not physically.

30:18.t: "Contrary to what was written": they ate it while unclean, which the Law forbade (Numbers 9:6).

"Seek" (Hebrew darash): darash means to seek, inquire of, or search out, and it is a key word in Chronicles: to seek the LORD is to turn to Him for guidance and to give Him one's worship and loyalty; to fail to seek Him is the heart of unfaithfulness (see 1 Chronicles 10:13-14). Hezekiah's prayer puts the heart that seeks God above ritual purity, and God answers it.

30:22.t: "Spoke encouragingly": the KJV's "spake comfortably", literally "spoke to the heart". "Who showed good understanding in the service": the KJV's "that taught the good knowledge"; the Hebrew can mean they had skill or taught well. "Giving thanks": the KJV's "making confession"; the Hebrew word means to praise or to confess.

30:24.t: KJV: "a thousand bullocks and seven thousand sheep ... a thousand bullocks and ten thousand sheep".

30:25.t: "Foreigners": the KJV's "strangers", non-Israelites living in the land; see 1 Chronicles 22:2.

31:1.t: "Sacred pillars", "Asherah poles": the KJV's "images" and "groves". Sacred pillars were standing stones used in Canaanite worship; Asherah was a Canaanite mother goddess, and her symbol was a wooden pole or carved tree set up beside an altar. See 14:3.

31:2.t: "The camp of the LORD": the KJV's "the tents of the LORD", an old name for the temple courts, recalling the camp in the wilderness (1 Chronicles 9:18-19).

31:4.t: "Devote themselves": the KJV's "be encouraged", literally "be strong in"; supported by the people, they could give their time to the Law.

31:5.t: "Grain": the KJV's "corn", meaning grain of any kind. "Honey": probably syrup from dates and other fruit as well as bees' honey.

31:7.t: From the third month (the grain harvest and Feast of Weeks) to the seventh (the fruit and grape harvest and Feast of Booths).

31:14.t: "Keeper of the East Gate": the KJV's "the porter toward the east". "Contributions": the KJV's "oblations".

31:15.t: "Faithfully": the KJV's "in their set office"; the Hebrew word means faithfulness or trust. See 1 Chronicles 9:22.

31:16.t: The Hebrew of these verses is difficult. They seem to say that the portions went to priests and Levites on duty and to their families listed in the genealogies.
"Three years old": some take this as "thirty years old", the age of service in Numbers 4:3, a one-letter difference in Hebrew.

31:19.t: "Pasturelands": the KJV's "suburbs", meaning the open land around a town used for grazing; see 1 Chronicles 5:16.

31:20.t: "Faithful": the KJV's "truth" (Hebrew emet), which means firmness, reliability, truth; see Genesis 24:27.

32:1.t: Compare 2 Kings 18:13-19:37 and Isaiah 36-37. Chronicles gives a shorter account and leaves out Hezekiah's payment of tribute (2 Kings 18:14-16).
"These acts of faithfulness": the KJV's "the establishment thereof"; the Hebrew emet means faithfulness. Sennacherib's invasion took place in 701 B.C.

32:4.t: "The stream that flowed through the land": the KJV's "the brook that ran through the midst of the land", probably the stream from the Gihon spring.

32:5.t: "Raised towers on it": the KJV's "raised it up to the towers". The Millo: a terraced structure or fill in the city of David; the name probably means "filling" (see 1 Chronicles 11:8). "Weapons": the KJV's "darts".

32:6.t: "The square at the city gate": the KJV's "the street of the gate". "Encouraged them": the KJV's "spake comfortably to them", literally "spoke to their heart"; see 30:22.

32:8.t: "An arm of flesh": human strength only.

32:12.t: "The LORD's high places and altars": the KJV's "his high places and his altars". The Assyrian means the shrines to Israel's God that Hezekiah removed (31:1).

32:18.t: "The language of Judah": the KJV's "the Jews' speech", Hebrew, as opposed to Aramaic, the language of diplomacy; see 2 Kings 18:26-28.

32:21.t: "Some of his own sons": the KJV's "they that came forth of his own bowels". 2 Kings 19:37 names them Adrammelech and Sharezer. He was killed about twenty years after the invasion, in 681 B.C. 2 Kings 19:35 gives the number of the Assyrian dead as 185,000.

32:22.t: "Gave them rest": the KJV's "guided them", following the printed Hebrew; some Hebrew copies and the Greek read "gave them rest", which is followed here.

32:24.t: Compare 2 Kings 20:1-11 and Isaiah 38, where the sign is the shadow going back on the stairway.

32:25.t: "The kindness shown him": the KJV's "the benefit done unto him", God's healing.

32:30.t: "Upper outlet of the waters of Gihon": Hezekiah's tunnel, about 530 meters long, cut through rock to bring water from the Gihon spring to the pool of Siloam inside the city. It can still be walked through, and an inscription found in it describes the digging.

32:31.t: "Sign": the KJV's "wonder", the sign of Hezekiah's healing (32:24). "Left him alone to test him": the KJV's "left him, to try him"; compare 2 Kings 20:12-19, where he shows the envoys all his treasures.

32:32.t: "Loyal deeds": the KJV's "goodness"; the Hebrew hasadim is the plural of hesed, loyal, committed love. A person's hesed is rendered "kindness" or "loyalty"; here it means Hezekiah's acts of devotion to God and to the temple. See the Original language note on 32:32.

"Loyal deeds" (Hebrew hasadim, plural of hesed): a person's hesed is rendered "kindness" or "loyalty" (see Genesis 24:27). Here it means his acts of devotion to God and to the temple. The same phrase is used of Josiah (35:26) and Nehemiah (Nehemiah 13:14).

32:33.t: "Upper part of the tombs": the KJV's "the chiefest of the sepulchres", the place of greatest honor.

33:1.t: Compare 2 Kings 21:1-18. Kings says nothing of Manasseh's captivity and repentance (33:11-17).

33:3.t: "The Baals": the KJV's "Baalim", the Hebrew plural, meaning local forms of Baal, the Canaanite storm and fertility god (baal means "lord" or "master") (see 17:3). "Asherah poles": the KJV's "groves"; Asherah was a Canaanite mother goddess, and her symbol was a wooden pole or carved tree set up beside an altar (see 14:3). "The host of heaven": the sun, moon, and stars worshiped as gods.

33:6.t: "Made his sons pass through the fire": child sacrifice by burning, in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, whose Hebrew name Ge-hinnom gave rise to Gehenna; see 28:3. "Fortune-telling, omens, and sorcery": the KJV's "observed times, and used enchantments, and used witchcraft". "Mediums and spiritists": the KJV's "a familiar spirit, and ... wizards", people who claimed to call up the dead; see 1 Chronicles 10:13.

33:7.t: "The carved image of the idol": 2 Kings 21:7 says it was an image of Asherah.

33:11.t: "With hooks": the KJV's "among the thorns"; the Hebrew word can mean either. Assyrian kings are shown leading captives by hooks through the nose or lips. "Bronze chains": the KJV's "fetters". Babylon was then under Assyrian rule.

33:12.t: "Sought the favor of", "was moved by his plea": the KJV's "besought" and "was intreated of him". A later Jewish writing, the Prayer of Manasseh, found in the Apocrypha, claims to be this prayer.

"Humbled himself" (Hebrew kana): kana means to bend low, to admit one's need before God; in Chronicles it marks the kings God spares (see 7:14). Manasseh, the worst of Judah's kings, is the clearest example in Chronicles of God answering one who humbles himself and prays. His son Amon did not, and Zedekiah (36:12) did not.

33:14.t: "Outer wall": the KJV's "a wall without". Ophel: the hill on the southeast side of Jerusalem, between the City of David and the temple (see 27:3).

33:19.t: "The records of the seers": the KJV's "the sayings of the seers"; the Hebrew may be read as a name, "the records of Hozai".

"Humbled himself" (Hebrew kana): kana means to bend low, to admit one's need before God; in Chronicles it marks the kings God spares (see 7:14). Manasseh, the worst of Judah's kings, is the clearest example in Chronicles of God answering one who humbles himself and prays. His son Amon did not, and Zedekiah (36:12) did not.

33:20.t: "In his own palace": 2 Kings 21:18 says in the garden of his palace, the garden of Uzza.

34:1.t: Compare 2 Kings 22:1-23:20. Kings puts the cleansing of the land after the finding of the book (18th year); Chronicles begins it in the 12th year.

34:3.t: "Seek" (Hebrew darash): darash means to seek, inquire of, or search out, and it is a key word in Chronicles: to seek the LORD is to turn to Him for guidance and to give Him one's worship and loyalty; to fail to seek Him is the heart of unfaithfulness (see 1 Chronicles 10:13-14). At sixteen Josiah began to seek the God of David, and the reforms followed.

34:4.t: "Incense altars": the KJV's "images" and "idols"; the Hebrew chammanim are probably incense stands. See 14:5.

34:7.t: "Incense altars": the KJV's "images" and "idols"; the Hebrew chammanim are probably incense stands. See 14:5.

34:6.t: "In the ruins all around them": the KJV's "with their mattocks round about". The Hebrew is unclear; it can be read "with their swords" or "in their ruins".

34:8.t: "Recorder": a royal official who kept the court records.

34:9.t: "Then they returned to Jerusalem": as in the KJV, following the written Hebrew text; the Hebrew margin reads "and the inhabitants of Jerusalem", completing the list of givers.

34:11.t: "Beams and rafters": the KJV's "couplings" and "floor". "Let fall into ruin": the KJV's "destroyed".

34:14.t: "The book of the law": probably Deuteronomy, or the whole Law of Moses.

34:20.t: Abdon the son of Micah: 2 Kings 22:12 has Achbor the son of Michaiah.

34:22.t: Tokhath, Hasrah: 2 Kings 22:14 has Tikvah and Harhas; the KJV's Tikvath. "Second Quarter": the KJV's "the college", a newer district of Jerusalem.

34:28.t: "In peace": Josiah died in battle (35:23-24), but before Jerusalem fell, so he did not see the disaster.

34:32.t: "Pledge themselves to it": the KJV's "stand to it".

35:3.t: "You no longer need to carry it on your shoulders": the KJV's "it shall not be a burden upon your shoulders". Why the ark was out of its place is not said; perhaps it had been removed under Manasseh or during the repairs.

35:5.t: "Lay people": the KJV's "the people". The Hebrew is difficult; the sense seems to be that Levites were assigned to each family group.

35:7.t: KJV: "thirty thousand, and three thousand bullocks".

35:8.t: "Chief officers": the KJV's "rulers". KJV: "two thousand and six hundred small cattle, and three hundred oxen".

35:9.t: Nethanel: the KJV spells it Nethaneel. KJV: "five thousand small cattle, and five hundred oxen".

35:13.t: "Roasted ... boiled": the KJV's "roasted ... sod". The Passover lamb had to be roasted (Exodus 12:8-9); other offerings were boiled. The Hebrew uses one verb, bashal, "cook", for both.

35:18.t: "Since the days of Samuel": 2 Kings 23:22 reads "from the days of the judges". Hezekiah's Passover (chapter 30) was in the second month and less in keeping with the Law.

35:20.t: Neco: the KJV's Necho, Pharaoh Neco II, who in 609 B.C. marched north to help the Assyrians against Babylon. Carchemish: a city on the upper Euphrates.

35:21.t: "The house with which I am at war": the ruling house of Babylon. "God": Neco may mean his own god, or Israel's God; the writer takes it as God's real word to Josiah (35:22).

35:22.t: "The plain of Megiddo": the KJV's "the valley of Megiddo", the plain of Jezreel.

35:24.t: 2 Kings 23:29-30 says he died at Megiddo and was brought dead to Jerusalem.

35:25.t: "The Laments": the KJV's "the lamentations", a collection of laments now lost, not the book of Lamentations, which mourns the fall of Jerusalem.

35:26.t: "Loyal deeds" (Hebrew hasadim, plural of hesed): the KJV's "goodness". Hesed is loyal, committed love; a person's hesed is rendered "kindness" or "loyalty". Here it means his acts of devotion to God and to the temple. See 32:32.

36:3.t: KJV: "an hundred talents of silver and a talent of gold".

36:6.t: 2 Kings 24:1-6 says Jehoiakim served Nebuchadnezzar, rebelled, and died in Jerusalem; whether he was actually taken to Babylon is not said there. Daniel 1:1-2 also tells of an early siege.

36:8.t: "What was found against him": the KJV's "that which was found in him".

36:9.t: "Eight years old": 2 Kings 24:8 reads eighteen, which fits better with his having wives (2 Kings 24:15); one Hebrew copy and the Greek read eighteen here.

36:10.t: "At the turn of the year": the KJV's "when the year was expired", in the spring; see 1 Chronicles 20:1. "His relative": the KJV's "his brother". 2 Kings 24:17 says Zedekiah was his uncle, a son of Josiah; the Hebrew "brother" can mean a relative.

36:13.t: "Stiffened his neck": a picture of stubbornness, like an ox that will not bend to the yoke.

36:15.t: "Again and again": the KJV's "rising up betimes, and sending", rising early to send them, a picture of God's persistent effort.

"Compassion" (Hebrew chamal): to have pity, to spare. God's patience is the reason for the long years of warning; when it was refused, "there was no remedy" (36:16). The same verb is used in 36:17 of the Chaldeans, who had none.

36:17.t: "Chaldeans": the KJV's "Chaldees", the people who ruled Babylon. "The aged": the KJV's "him that stooped for age".

36:20.t: Jerusalem fell in 586 B.C.; Persia conquered Babylon in 539 B.C.

36:21.t: "Enjoyed its Sabbaths": the land rested as the Law required every seventh year (Leviticus 25:1-7, 26:34-35), years Israel had not kept. Seventy years: Jeremiah 25:11-12, 29:10.

36:22.t: These verses are repeated in Ezra 1:1-3, linking the two books; the wording here matches our Ezra 1:1-3. The Hebrew Bible ends with these words, "let him go up".

6:21.t: "Forgive" (Hebrew salach): used only of God in the Old Testament, it means to pardon, to remove guilt so that the relationship is restored. The prayer asks again and again for this, on condition that the people turn back (shuv, to turn around or come back, used both of repentance and of returning from exile; see 1 Kings 8:47-48).

7:14.t: "Humble themselves", "seek My face", "turn" (Hebrew kana, biqqesh panai, shuv): kana means to bend low, to admit one's need before God; in Chronicles it marks the kings God spares (12:6-7, 32:26, 33:12). "Seek My face" (biqqesh, a close partner of darash, to seek, inquire of, turn to God for guidance; see 1 Chronicles 10:13-14) means to come into God's presence in prayer and worship. "Turn" (shuv, to turn around or come back; see 1 Kings 8:47-48) is the Old Testament word for repentance. The promise was spoken to Israel about this temple and this land; readers also take it as a pattern for how God answers His people in every age, and both readings are common.

"Heal their land" (Hebrew rapha): to heal, restore or make whole, used of bodies, land and nations (see Exodus 15:26). The setting is drought, locusts and plague (7:13), so healing the land means restoring its rain and harvests.

12:6.t: "Humbled themselves" (Hebrew kana): kana means to bend low, to admit one's need before God; in Chronicles it marks the kings God spares (see 7:14). This is the first test of that promise: even a king who had abandoned the LORD is spared, in part, when he bows low.

12:14.t: "Seek" (Hebrew darash): darash means to seek, inquire of, or search out, and it is a key word in Chronicles: to seek the LORD is to turn to Him for guidance and to give Him one's worship and loyalty; to fail to seek Him is the heart of unfaithfulness (see 1 Chronicles 10:13-14). The writer gives the root of Rehoboam's failure: he did not set his heart to seek the LORD.

14:4.t: "Seek" (Hebrew darash, also biqqesh in 15:4 and 15:15): darash means to seek, inquire of, or search out, and it is a key word in Chronicles: to seek the LORD is to turn to Him for guidance and to give Him one's worship and loyalty; to fail to seek Him is the heart of unfaithfulness (see 1 Chronicles 10:13-14). In Asa's story "seek" sounds again and again: the king calls Judah to seek the LORD, and the prophet promises that those who seek Him will find Him. When Asa later relies on Aram and seeks only physicians (16:7, 16:12), the same word marks his decline.

15:12.t: "Seek" (Hebrew darash, also biqqesh in 15:4 and 15:15): darash means to seek, inquire of, or search out, and it is a key word in Chronicles: to seek the LORD is to turn to Him for guidance and to give Him one's worship and loyalty; to fail to seek Him is the heart of unfaithfulness (see 1 Chronicles 10:13-14). In Asa's story "seek" sounds again and again: the king calls Judah to seek the LORD, and the prophet promises that those who seek Him will find Him. When Asa later relies on Aram and seeks only physicians (16:7, 16:12), the same word marks his decline.

18:20.t: "A lying spirit" (Hebrew ruach sheqer): ruach means spirit, wind and breath (see Genesis 1:2). The scene pictures the LORD's heavenly council, and the prophet reports that God has allowed the false prophets to be deceived as judgment on a king who would not hear the truth. Readers differ over whether this is a vision in picture language or a literal account; both see that God is in control and that Ahab was warned plainly.

20:3.t: "Seek" (Hebrew darash, biqqesh): darash means to seek, inquire of, or search out, and it is a key word in Chronicles: to seek the LORD is to turn to Him for guidance and to give Him one's worship and loyalty; to fail to seek Him is the heart of unfaithfulness (see 1 Chronicles 10:13-14). Jehoshaphat's whole kingdom seeks the LORD together, with fasting and prayer, the clearest picture of 7:14 in action.

20:20.t: "Believe ... and you will be established" (Hebrew haaminu ... teamenu): both verbs come from the root aman, "to be firm" (the source of "amen"). The wordplay means "Stand firm in the LORD, and you will stand firm". Isaiah 7:9 uses the same play.

25:2.t: "A whole heart" (Hebrew lev shalem, the KJV's "a perfect heart"): shalem, from the same root as shalom, means whole, complete, undivided, not sinless (see 16:9). Amaziah obeyed outwardly but his heart was divided, which the rest of the chapter shows.

25:15.t: "Sought" (Hebrew darash): darash means to seek, inquire of, or search out, and it is a key word in Chronicles: to seek the LORD is to turn to Him for guidance and to give Him one's worship and loyalty; to fail to seek Him is the heart of unfaithfulness (see 1 Chronicles 10:13-14). Amaziah sought the gods of Edom instead of the LORD, the reverse of the call to seek Him.

25:20.t: "Sought" (Hebrew darash): darash means to seek, inquire of, or search out, and it is a key word in Chronicles: to seek the LORD is to turn to Him for guidance and to give Him one's worship and loyalty; to fail to seek Him is the heart of unfaithfulness (see 1 Chronicles 10:13-14). Amaziah sought the gods of Edom instead of the LORD, the reverse of the call to seek Him.

32:26.t: "Humbled himself" (Hebrew kana): kana means to bend low, to admit one's need before God; in Chronicles it marks the kings God spares (see 7:14). Hezekiah's pride after his healing is met with humility, and the threatened wrath is held back in his lifetime.

33:23.t: "Humbled himself" (Hebrew kana): kana means to bend low, to admit one's need before God; in Chronicles it marks the kings God spares (see 7:14). Manasseh, the worst of Judah's kings, is the clearest example in Chronicles of God answering one who humbles himself and prays. His son Amon did not, and Zedekiah (36:12) did not.

34:27.t: "Your heart was tender" (Hebrew rakh levavekha): in Hebrew the heart is the center of thought, will and character, not mainly the feelings (see 1 Samuel 16:7). A tender heart is soft, able to be moved and to respond, the opposite of the hardened heart of Zedekiah (36:13).
